items.prompt: A learner writes: “Secondary industry means second-hand trading, such as selling used boat engines.” Explain the error, then classify catching hake, canning pilchards and selling used engines.
items.canonical_answer: Secondary does not mean second-hand: it is the processing or manufacturing of raw materials into products. Catching hake is primary because it extracts a natural resource, canning pilchards is secondary because it processes fish, and selling used engines is tertiary because it is a trade service, whatever the age of the goods.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for identifying the error: secondary means processing or manufacturing, not second-hand goods.
1 mark for the correct classification used as a test: catching hake primary, canning pilchards secondary, selling used engines tertiary.

items.prompt: Explain the link from coastal upwelling off Namibia to a useful fish resource.
items.canonical_answer: South-east trade winds push surface water away from Namibia’s coast, so cold, nutrient-rich water rises from depth into the sunlit surface layer. The nutrients support rapid phytoplankton growth. Zooplankton and fish feed on this production through the food chain, so large fish stocks can be supported over time.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that Namibia’s fisheries management has made its fish resources sustainable?
items.canonical_answer: Agree to some extent. Since 1990 the 200-nautical-mile EEZ has ended uncontrolled foreign fishing, and fishing rights, licences and yearly TACs set from scientific advice limit the catch. Observers on every commercial vessel, patrols and inspection of landings make the limits enforceable, while closed seasons and minimum mesh sizes protect breeding and young fish. However, rules cannot control the ocean: the 1993–1995 Benguela Niño, on top of earlier overfishing, reduced pilchard so far that its quota was set at zero for 2002. Quotas also protect stocks only if they are set at the right level and obeyed. Decision: management is strong and has protected most stocks, but environmental shocks mean sustainability is not guaranteed.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging relevant evidence on both sides: EEZ control; rights, licences and TACs; observers and patrols; closed seasons or mesh rules; the pilchard decline from the Benguela Niño and earlier overfishing; quotas needing correct levels and compliance.
1 C mark for a supported decision, which may be implied.

items.prompt:
![Flow diagram of an invented fish-processing plant: inputs entering a dashed plant boundary, six processing steps, and three output flows with daily quantities and destinations](../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.1-038-INTERP-question.png)

Describe the input–process–output relationships in this processing-system diagram, using its boundary and labelled material/service flows.
items.canonical_answer:
Fish (10 t a day) and supporting resources – water, electricity, workers and packaging – enter the plant boundary. Inside it the fish are received, cleaned and gutted, filleted, frozen, graded and packed, then cold-stored. Outputs leave to different destinations: 4 t of frozen fillet packs to buyers, 5 t of heads, frames and skins to a fishmeal plant, and 1 t of trimmings and liquid to wastewater treatment.

marking_guidance: 1 mark for the input feature; 1 for the transforming-stage evidence; 1 for the output/destination relationship.

items.prompt: Explain how Namibia’s policy of promoting onshore fish processing supports sustainable development.
items.canonical_answer: Much of the hake catch must be landed fresh for processing on shore, so filleting and packing take place in Walvis Bay and Lüderitz rather than at sea. This creates jobs and skills for Namibians and adds value before export, so more income from each tonne stays in the country. Because the catch is already limited by TACs, extra benefit comes from processing rather than from catching more fish, supporting people now while protecting stocks for the future.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the factor: required onshore processing of part of the catch; 1 for the link: local jobs, skills and value added; 1 for the link because the catch is capped by TACs; 1 for the effect: more benefit without increasing catch, supporting long-term use.

items.prompt:
A hypothetical processor compares sites. Monthly inbound delivery, outbound dispatch and energy costs are respectively A: N$48,000, N$12,000 and N$20,000; B: N$74,000, N$9,000 and N$18,000. No other cost or revenue is supplied.
(a) Name the location factor represented by dispatch costs. [1]
(b) Calculate the total of the three supplied monthly costs at A. [2]
(c) Describe three contrasts between the sites using this resource. [3]
(d) What decision about the claim “A must be more profitable” is supported? [1]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Transport. (b) 48,000+12,000+20,000 = N$80,000 per month. (c) A has N$26,000 lower inbound cost, but N$3,000 higher dispatch and N$2,000 higher energy costs. Its supplied total is N$21,000 below B’s N$101,000. Credit any three distinct supported comparisons. (d) A has a lower supplied partial cost total, but profit cannot be established without revenue and remaining costs.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for transport.
(b) 2 B marks for the addition method and correct monthly total with currency.
(c) 3 B marks for three different comparative patterns using resource evidence and values; do not credit the same comparison twice.
(d) 1 C mark for a supported decision distinguishing partial costs from profit.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that a quota on paper proves sustainable fishing? In this hypothetical simplified stock account, opening stock is 100 units, net natural addition before fishing is 40 units, and actual removal is 60 units; other stock changes are stated absent. The operator observes its 60-unit quota and reports jobs. Judge maintained stock and the wider sustainability claim. [5]
items.canonical_answer: Disagree that those facts prove sustainability. Closing stock is 80 units, a decline of 20 despite quota compliance. This quota is therefore not sufficient to maintain stock under the stated conditions; the permitted removal and its scientific basis need reassessment. Jobs are a development benefit but do not establish recovery, ecosystem condition or future livelihood security. Monitoring, an appropriate limit and effective enforcement are relevant together. The simplified stock balance supports a decline for this interval, not a complete prediction of the real fishery.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging the 100+40−60 balance, the compliant-but-inappropriate limit, employment evidence and the missing wider ecological/longer-term evidence.
1 C mark for a supported overall decision distinguishing a stated rule from observed sustainable performance.
